metadata.title: ECIS — Episode 5: The System That Learned From Its Own Mistakes

beats.narration_text: Four episodes in, ECIS could read an earnings call. This week it did something harder — it read its own mistakes. I'm Anjana. Here's what the system learned about itself.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Hello, Anjana'; ask types itself
runningText 'reviewing this week's errors…'
output lines resolve: 'fine-tuned on its own corrections' / 'penalties that scale with disagreement' / 'every signal now has a shelf life'

props.command: Last time, ECIS weighted every signal by who said it and how clean the source was. This week you went back through its errors and retrained on the one boundary it kept getting wrong. Can you show me what changed?
output: every signal now has a shelf life

beats.narration_text: ECIS is a system that reads earnings call transcripts and extracts financial guidance signals automatically. It runs four independent readers on every chunk of every transcript: keyword matching, FinBERT sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and a large language model. A triangulator fuses their outputs. Every signal is pre-registered before anyone knows the outcome, then graded against the market at thirty, ninety, and one hundred eighty days. The system does not trust any single reader or any single confidence number. It triangulates, scores, and self-corrects. That is the foundation. Here is what it learned this week.

show.event: a transcript document enters from the left and splits into chunks
four reader nodes light up in narration order — Keyword (blue), FinBERT (teal), NER (orange), LLM (purple)
arrows from all four converge into the Triangulator; one signal exits with a direction + confidence badge
the signal drops into an append-only log and a padlock stamps onto it — pre-registered
a timeline extends right with 30 / 90 / 180-day checkpoints; each grades green or red against the market
on 'That is the foundation' the whole architecture settles into a compact overview

beats.narration_text: The hardest call in the pipeline was the line between maintained and none. The system kept confusing "we are comfortable with our outlook" with "we remain focused on execution." One is guidance reaffirmed. The other is not guidance at all. So human-reviewed extractions were formatted into training data, concentrated on that exact boundary. A QLoRA adapter was trained on top of the base eight billion parameter model. Rank sixteen adapters, four-bit quantization, five epochs. The adapter does not replace the model. It sharpens the one edge where it was weakest.

show.event: two quote cards land side by side — 'comfortable with our current outlook' tagged MAINTAINED (blue), 'remain focused on execution' tagged NONE (grey)
a red decision-boundary zone pulses between them, scattered with red X marks — past misclassifications
the cards shrink into a stream of training examples flowing into the base model; counter reads '200+ reviewed extractions'
a small QLoRA adapter block glows beside the much larger base model — 'Rank 16 · 4-bit · 5 epochs'
the adapter locks into the model's side; both quotes are re-read and tagged correctly with higher confidence
the red X marks clear to green checkmarks; label lands: 'Same model. Sharper edge.'

beats.narration_text: Self-consistency runs the same prompt three times and votes. Before, a two-to-one vote always got the same flat penalty. But a close disagreement is not the same as a wide one. Now the penalty scales with the spread. If the majority says zero point eight and the minority says zero point seven five, the penalty is small. If the majority says zero point eight and the minority says zero point two, the penalty is large. And on top of that, where the signal came from matters. Prepared remarks carry full weight. Q&A carries zero point eight. Rehearsed language is more reliable than spontaneous answers.

show.event: the close-vote panel builds: maintained 0.80, maintained 0.78, raised 0.75, with a '2/3 agree' tag
a thin arrow nudges confidence 0.80 → 0.77; green border; 'Small spread. Small penalty.'
the wide-vote panel builds beside it: maintained 0.80, maintained 0.82, raised 0.20 — the same '2/3 agree' tag
a thick arrow pushes 0.80 → 0.62; amber border; 'Large spread. Large penalty.'
a transcript splits horizontally: Prepared Remarks with a green 1.0 badge, Q&A with an amber 0.8 badge
the equation lands: 0.75 × 0.8 = 0.60 — 'Rehearsed vs spontaneous.'

beats.narration_text: Three new detection layers. First, negation detection. Phrases like "not raising," "won't increase," "does not expect" now force full extraction regardless of fast-pass results. FinBERT handles negation inconsistently, so negated chunks skip the shortcut and go straight to the LLM. Second, keyword density. A chunk packed with guidance phrases is a strong explicit signal. A chunk with no keyword matches but a FinBERT flag is sentiment-only, and less reliable. Third, duplicate detection. Re-filed transcripts get caught by matching and skipped. No inflated signal counts, no wasted compute.

show.event: detector 1 — the chunk 'We do not expect to raise guidance this quarter.' appears; 'do not expect to raise' highlights red and a negation flag lands
a routing diagram shows the chunk bypassing the fast-pass lane straight to full LLM extraction
detector 2 — two chunks side by side; the left fills its density meter to 0.85 green, the right barely reaches 0.05 red with only a FinBERT tag
the left chunk's arrow to the triangulator is thick; the right's is thin and faded
detector 3 — two identical transcript icons with matching hashes; the second is stamped DUPLICATE and greys out
counter reads 'Skipped. Compute saved.'

beats.narration_text: Not all predictions age the same way. A signal can be right at thirty days and wrong at one hundred eighty. That is a decaying signal, short-term noise that looked real. A signal that is right at all three horizons is persistent, a genuine read. Now every signal carries a decay profile. The scorecard knows which readers produce lasting predictions and which ones fade.

show.event: Company A's signal card lands: 'raised, 0.84', with a timeline running right
checkpoints grade in order — 30 days green check, 90 days amber question mark, 180 days red X
its confidence bar fades green → red along the timeline; tag: 'Decaying. Short-term noise.'
Company B's card appears below: 'lowered, 0.79'
all three of its checkpoints grade green; the bar stays solid; tag: 'Persistent. Genuine read.'
both visible together; label: 'Same confidence. Different shelf life.'

beats.narration_text: Five weight dimensions. Three horizons. One fine-tuned model. ECIS, episode five.

show.event: flash 1 — five weight bars stack vertically: Reader, Model, Speaker, Quality, Section
flash 2 — the 30 / 90 / 180 timeline with three green checkmarks
flash 3 — the base model with its small QLoRA adapter attached
all fade; the title lands: ECIS — Episode 5

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The model was fine-tuned on its own reviewed errors, sharpened on the one boundary it kept missing. Disagreement penalties now scale with how far apart the votes actually are. Three new detectors catch negation, weak lexical support, and duplicate filings before they reach the scorecard. And every signal now carries a decay profile across all three horizons. The system did not get bigger this week. It got more honest about where it was wrong.

show.event: 0.5s lead pause, then ClaudeVerdictArtifact card builds in
line 1: the fine-tune line settles in
line 2: the spread-scaled penalty line settles in
line 3: the three-detector line settles in
line 4: the decay-profile line locks in, largest element

props.artifactHeading: It got more honest about where it was wrong.
artifactLines: A QLoRA adapter, trained on reviewed errors, sharpens the maintained-vs-none boundary.
Disagreement penalties now scale with the spread between majority and minority votes.
Negation, keyword density, and duplicate detection gate chunks before the scorecard.
Every signal carries a decay profile across 30, 90, and 180 days.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. "I have a judgment call I make repeatedly where I keep getting the same specific type of case wrong — not randomly wrong, wrong in one consistent direction on one particular kind of input. Can you help me: one, name the exact boundary where my judgment breaks down, as precisely as I can define it; two, design a way to collect and review my own past calls on just that boundary so I have real examples of the mistake rather than a vague sense of it; and three, tell me honestly whether a targeted fix on that one edge would help more than trying to get generally better at the whole task?" Paste that into Claude and find the one edge where your own judgment is weakest.

show.event: ClaudeComposerAsk: greeting 'Your turn.'; prompt types itself into the composer
runningText 'finding your weakest edge…'
